prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active forms, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed GLP-1 first, and the agreement rests on the evidence rather than on habit. The chain from proglucagon processing and incretin physiology to receptor biology, stable agonists and large randomized outcome trials is unusually complete and independently confirmed. The effect on type 2 diabetes, obesity and cardiometabolic and renal risk is very large and still growing. Recognition is timely, arguably overdue. The academic physiology and peptide-identification contributions (Holst, Drucker, Mojsov) form a coherent discovery achievement that a three-person prize can honor without difficulty.
statement.case_against: Credit allocation is the real weakness. Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-37)/(7-36) forms is contested, and Habener is not among the credited names. The three-person cap leaves out Knudsen, whose medicinal chemistry produced the long-acting agonists that reached patients. A prize built on the physiology could be read as passing over the people who made the clinical impact possible. If the committee wanted to honor translation, this configuration would be the wrong one.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked GLP-1 first with the three academic names, arguing that a prize centered on the discovery of the hormone's action is better served without Knudsen. He placed the unfolded protein response (B040) second as a clean Walter and Mori pairing, and ranked optogenetics (B012) only sixth because medicine favors direct impact on health.
responses.response: I agree with the three-name core and with leaving Knudsen out, but I do not think the exclusion is cost-free: the disputed priority around the active peptide is a weakness of the academic trio that we should state openly. On B040 I largely share his view. The Ire1-Hac1/XBP1 mechanism is clean, the pair is compact, and credit is clearer than for most candidates. I would qualify his medicine argument in one respect. B040 has less clinical translation than the therapeutic candidates, so I treat it as the strongest basic-science alternative rather than as a competitor to B019. His lower ranking of B012 on medical-relevance grounds is fair, though I would not reduce its worth to the tool alone.

responses.point: El-Manira ranked optogenetics (B012) second with Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann, arguing that it transformed causal circuit neuroscience and physiology, and he accepts that the six-name credit list forces a hard allocation that omits Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck.
responses.response: I agree on the scale of the discovery, and I also placed it second. But I cannot give it my preferred slot because of the allocation problem he describes, which I think is more serious than he suggests. Nagel and Hegemann for channelrhodopsin and Deisseroth for neuronal deployment is defensible, but Boyden's contemporaneous neuronal demonstration and Bamberg's earlier work are real priority claims. A prize that picks among them would be contested for years. Unlike GLP-1, where the dispute is at the margin (Habener, Mojsov), here the dispute is at the core. The clinical case is still limited to early retinal work. That makes me put B012 behind B019 and, narrowly, behind B040 as a cleaner configuration.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked GLP-1 first but said that Knudsen's drug-design contribution would be the first person left out, and that credit between basic and drug-development contributions is unresolved. He ranked CAR-T (B030) third and noted that Eshhar's original chimeric receptor concept is not among the credited names.
responses.response: I share his reservation about Knudsen and have no better solution than the academic trio, but I want the discussion to record that the omission is a deliberate choice, not an oversight. On B030, I agree that missing Eshhar weakens the credited trio. I would go further: I trimmed June and Sadelain to two in my opening ballot because Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is a different achievement from CAR engineering. If CAR-T advances, we should decide whether the prize is for CAR engineering (June, Sadelain) or for cell therapy more broadly, and that choice changes who is credited. Until that is settled it remains my third alternative, not a rival to GLP-1.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked GLP-1 first and listed cGAS-STING (B024) seventh with Chen, Barber and Ishikawa, noting that mechanism is well confirmed but therapeutic benefit is not yet established and that credit between group leaders and trainees in the Chen laboratory is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree that the trainee question is the central attribution issue for B024. Chen's discovery of cGAS and cGAMP is decisive and Barber's STING work is independent, so I see Chen and Barber as the stable core and would not extend the prize to the laboratory co-authors by default. Her point about unproven clinical benefit is where I would press harder: for a prize in this field, mechanism alone is strong enough only when the conceptual advance is as clean as the unfolded protein response. For cGAS-STING I think the case is currently one to two cycles early, and I did not place it in my top eight.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide, given Habener's absence from the credited names and my recollection that the claim is contested; I cannot verify the details from the supplied files.
Whether a physiology-centered GLP-1 prize without Knudsen will be judged to under-credit the clinical translation, which would favor a different three-person split.
Whether B040 should be preferred over any therapeutic candidate if the committee weighs conceptual originality above clinical impact.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. My profile records co-authorship with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisen and a postdoctoral period in Christopher Burge's group, but none of them is a credited name on the shortlist. My work on RNA processing and splicing is topically near B028, but topic proximity alone does not establish a conflict, and B028 is not in my preferred configuration.
